parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: Steam across the water
parts.subtitle: A look at the early history of boats powered by steam
parts.article:
Steam across the water

(A) During the 1600s, very early in the development of steam engines, inventive spirits like the Frenchman Denis Papin dreamed of - and experimented with - boats driven by steam, rather than by the wind or human effort, but many decades passed before those visions became reality.

(B) Englishman Jonathan Hulls took out patents on a steamboat in 1736, but it was to be driven by a Newcomen engine, which was heavy and therefore inefficient, and would never be a success. In 1763, William Henry, an American, put a Watt steam engine in a boat, but it sank. Nearly 20 years later, in the 1780s, a steam-powered paddle-wheeler managed to last fifteen minutes against the current on the River Saone in France, but lacked the endurance for longer trips. Developments elsewhere included a boat driven by a steam-powered water-jet and able to do six kilometres per hour. However, all these steamboats were either too slow or too expensive to run. For example, American John Fitch successfully trialled his first steamboat in 1787, but although he tried a number of designs and solved many technical challenges - one of his boats could even travel at 13 km/h - he could never convince sceptics that steamboats would pay.

(C) The 19th century came before real success could be claimed. In Scotland in 1802, Lord Dundas launched the steamboat Charlotte Dundas, which was driven by a paddle wheel and had an improved engine designed by William Symington. Barges, some weighing as much as 70 tonnes, were towed by this steamboat 30 kilometres along the Forth and Clyde Canal to Glasgow, Scotland’s second city. Soon after, success came to American Robert Fulton, whose countrymen called him "the father of the steamboat". Inspired by news of the Charlotte Dundas, Fulton ran steamboat trials on the River Seine, in an attempt to attract French support for his submarine Nautilus. He later imported a Boulton-Watt steam engine and built a boat to use it in. In 1807, the Clermont began a scheduled passenger steamboat service between New York and Albany, 250 kilometres up the Hudson River, taking 30 hours for the trip. Within a few years, steamers were running on the St Lawrence River in Canada and would soon appear on other rivers and lakes, including the Mississippi River, a most famous venue for the paddle-wheelers.

(D) Back in Scotland, Fulton’s ideas inspired Henry Bell, who launched his Comet in 1812 on the Clyde between Glasgow and Greenock. Inside a decade, dozens of steamboats were to be seen on the rivers, lochs and canals of Scotland, carrying cargo and occasionally passengers. The age of steamboats had come.

(E) Once steamboats were carrying passengers and industrial goods along the inland waterways and sheltered coastlines of Europe, North America and elsewhere, the challenge became to send steamboats onto the open ocean, such as across the Atlantic Ocean, between Europe and the US. Travelling under steam power alone would require engines to use less coal so the ship could stay at sea for several weeks. In order to provide a reliable service, it was also necessary to replace paddle wheels as a source of power with something less affected by the rolling of the ship.

(F) Without waiting for such breakthroughs, crossings under a combination of steam and sail got underway in 1819 with the American ship Savannah. A regular service took another two decades and introduced the famous name of Cunard. Securing the British government contract for the mail service across the Atlantic, Samuel Cunard established a shipping line in 1840, soon carrying passengers as well, and offering guaranteed sailing dates. Cunard’s first ships used a sail-steam combination, but the era of the passenger liner, using steam alone, was getting close. When it came to building the ships, the versatile British engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel set the pace. Brunel, brilliant and daring, had already built the Great Western Railway. He created ever bigger ships - faster, more luxurious and comfortable for passengers. The Great Western, launched in 1838, was 70 metres long and crossed from Bristol to New York in just fifteen days. The largest paddle steamer ever built was Brunel’s Great Eastern. Ultimately too expensive to run as a passenger ship, it was leased to lay the first submarine telegraph cable from Europe to America. His 1853 Great Britain, nearly 100 metres long and luxuriously appointed, was the first ocean-going steamship made of iron, and the first to use the underwater screw propeller for powering movement in place of paddle wheels. The idea of the screw had been around since the experiments of the American John Stevens in 1803, but only in 1838 did a large steamer use one, the riverboat Archimedes built by Francis Pettit Smith. Later ships had twin screws for reliability.

(G) In many modern ships, steam turbines have replaced engines with pistons, with fuel oil instead of coal to fire the boilers. Diesel engines keep others moving. The largest ships afloat now would dwarf Brunel’s Great Eastern, launched in 1860; the Atlantic can be crossed in only four days. But in whatever form, the ever-evolving descendants of the original visions of Denis Papin and Robert Fulton continue to travel the seas in vast numbers.

groups.contentHtml:
1 The engine of Jonathan Hulls’ steamboat was due to its weight.
2 A French paddle steamer did not have the to keep going for more than a quarter of an hour.
3 John Fitch overcame a number of problems with his steamboat designs.
4 In France, Fulton used a steamboat to try to raise interest in a .
5 Passengers in the US began to be carried regularly by a steamboat called the .
6 In Scotland, steamboats transported some passengers, but mostly .

analyses.content: 原文明确提到因为发动机很重（heavy），所以导致了“inefficient”（效率低下）的结果，填入即可。
你可能会想填“heavy”，但题目中已经写了“due to its weight”（因为它的重量），再填heavy意思就重复了。
Englishman Jonathan Hulls took out patents on a steamboat in 1736, but it was to be driven by a Newcomen engine, which was heavy and therefore inefficient, and would never be a success.
原文说这艘法国船只坚持了15分钟，缺乏进行更长旅行的“endurance”（耐力），刚好对应题目中的“无法继续行驶超过一刻钟”。
你可能会在原文找否定词“did not have”，但这里原文用了意思相同的“lacked”（缺乏）来替换，别被形式骗了。
Nearly 20 years later, in the 1780s, a steam-powered paddle-wheeler managed to last fifteen minutes against the current on the River Saone in France, but lacked the endurance for longer trips.
原文提到John Fitch解决了很多“technical”（技术的）挑战，这里的挑战（challenges）就对应题目中的克服问题（problems）。
你可能被后面的速度数字“13”吸引，但题目要填的是修饰“problems”的词，对应原文找修饰“challenges”的词就行。

For example, American John Fitch successfully trialled his first steamboat in 1787, but although he tried a number of designs and solved many technical challenges - one of his boats could even travel at 13 km/h - he could never convince sceptics that steamboats would pay.
原文清楚写着Fulton做实验是为了试图吸引法国人对他“submarine”（潜水艇）的支持，对应题目中的“提高兴趣”。
你可能会想填“Nautilus”（鹦鹉螺号），但题目只需要填这东西的种类，且Nautilus是专有名词，submarine更符合语法。
Inspired by news of the Charlotte Dundas, Fulton ran steamboat trials on the River Seine, in an attempt to attract French support for his submarine Nautilus.
原文提到开始定期（scheduled）提供客运服务（passenger steamboat service）的船名叫“Clermont”。
你可能会去原文找带引号或长得奇怪的词，但只要定位到美国地点和“客运服务”，直接拿对应的船名即可。
In 1807, the Clermont began a scheduled passenger steamboat service between New York and Albany, 250 kilometres up the Hudson River, taking 30 hours for the trip.
原文提到苏格兰的蒸汽船运送“cargo”（货物），偶尔（occasionally）也运乘客，也就是题目说的“大部分运送货物”。
你可能会不小心填成“passengers”，但原文说了运乘客是“偶尔的”（occasionally），主要运的当然是前面的“cargo”。
Inside a decade, dozens of steamboats were to be seen on the rivers, lochs and canals of Scotland, carrying cargo and occasionally passengers.

questions.question: For steamboats to cross the Atlantic Ocean, engines which used fuel economically were needed.

analyses.content: 原文明确说跨洋航行需要发动机少用煤（use less coal），也就是题目说的经济地使用燃料（economically），意思完全一样。
你可能会因为没看到“economically”原词就选NOT GIVEN，但“少用煤”就是节约燃料最直白的同义替换。

Once steamboats were carrying passengers... the challenge became to send steamboats onto the open ocean... Travelling under steam power alone would require engines to use less coal so the ship could stay at sea for several weeks.

questions.question: Using paddle wheels guaranteed reliability on ocean crossings.

analyses.content: 原文说为了保证服务可靠，必须把明轮（paddle wheels）替换掉（replace），说明它根本无法保证可靠性，和题目说的“保证了可靠性”截然相反。
你可能会看到原文同时出现了“reliable”和“paddle wheels”就选了YES，但一定要看清前面的动词是“必须替换掉它”。
In order to provide a reliable service, it was also necessary to replace paddle wheels as a source of power with something less affected by the rolling of the ship.

questions.question: The Savannah was much faster than a regular paddle steamer.

analyses.content: 原文只说Savannah号用了蒸汽和风帆的混合动力，压根没把它和普通的明轮船比速度。
你可能会自己脑补混合动力的船一定跑得更快，但在阅读考试里，原文没比就是没比。
Without waiting for such breakthroughs, crossings under a combination of steam and sail got underway in 1819 with the American ship Savannah.

questions.question: Brunel preferred designing railways to steamships.

analyses.content: 原文确实夸了Brunel建了铁路，也建了更棒的蒸汽船，但根本没说他“更偏爱”（preferred）哪一个。
你可能会因为原文先说他建了铁路，就以为这是他的最爱，实际上原文只是在客观列举成就，没有做偏好对比。

When it came to building the ships, the versatile British engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel set the pace. Brunel, brilliant and daring, had already built the Great Western Railway. He created ever bigger ships - faster, more luxurious and comfortable for passengers.

questions.question: The Great Britain had more than one innovative feature.

analyses.content: 原文说大不列颠号是“第一艘”铁制远洋船，也是“第一艘”用水下螺旋桨的，有两个“第一”，完美符合题目说的“不止一个创新特征”。
你可能会因为找不到“innovative”（创新的）这个词而纠结，其实原文连用两个“the first”，意思就是这是创新。

His 1853 Great Britain, nearly 100 metres long and luxuriously appointed, was the first ocean-going steamship made of iron, and the first to use the underwater screw propeller for powering movement in place of paddle wheels.

questions.question: The design of the riverboat Archimedes was widely admired.

analyses.content: 原文只是说明阿基米德号是一艘用了螺旋桨的大船，根本没提它的设计有没有“受到广泛赞赏”（widely admired）。
你可能会觉得第一个用螺旋桨的大船肯定很受赞赏，切记不要用自己的常识去推断原文没写的内容。
The idea of the screw had been around since the experiments of the American John Stevens in 1803, but only in 1838 did a large steamer use one, the riverboat Archimedes built by Francis Pettit Smith.

questions.question: Modern ships that cross the Atlantic use the same energy source as the early steamships.

analyses.content: 原文明确说现代船只用燃油（fuel oil）代替了煤炭（coal），说明能源变了，题目却说使用了“相同（same）”的能源，直接冲突。
你可能会看到句首还有“steam”（蒸汽）字样就以为能源没变，但后面明确写了燃料变成了燃油（instead of coal）。
In many modern ships, steam turbines have replaced engines with pistons, with fuel oil instead of coal to fire the boilers.
